query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of tungsten into the CoCrFeNi matrix will induce beneficial lattice distortion and nucleate W-rich secondary phases that trigger the in situ formation of a continuous, protective tribo‐oxide glaze layer during sliding. This adaptive wear‐protection mechanism is expected to reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix produced by standard synthesis routes (e.g., casting or powder metallurgy) without additional alloying for wear improvement.
generation.intervention: Microalloying the system with approximately 0.5 at.% tungsten added into the CoCrFeNi composition.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tribological tests conducted over a wide temperature range (from room temperature up to 800 °C) under moderate loads and speeds representative of typical engineering applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The tungsten addition is expected to create lattice distortion and promote the formation of W-rich intermetallic or secondary phases that act as nucleation sites for a dense, adherent oxide glaze layer during sliding, thereby acting as a structural mediator between the underlying metallic matrix and the evolving tribolayer.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures the unchanged ductile matrix provides low shear strength; under elevated temperatures, the induced lattice distortion and W-rich phase precipitates catalyze tribo-oxidation, leading to the rapid formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline oxide (glaze) layer. This layer protects the metal from severe adhesive or abrasive mechanisms and maintains low friction and wear rates over the full temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the tungsten-alloyed version is predicted to show a more stable and lower coefficient of friction and a significantly reduced wear rate across both room temperature and high-temperature (up to 800 °C) regimes. The beneficial effect will be particularly pronounced at elevated temperatures where protective oxide layer formation is critical.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix without tungsten addition.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under dry sliding conditions with similar counterpart materials, moderate contact loads, and sliding speeds; environmental conditions should range from ambient to 800 °C in the absence of additional lubricants or atmospheres that might independently alter tribochemical reactions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal tungsten concentration and detailed phase evolution during high-temperature sliding are not fully quantified. Uncertainties remain regarding long-term cyclic stability and potential microstructural changes (e.g., phase coarsening or unstable intermetallic formation) that could mitigate the intended lubricious effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using an identical processing route: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and a second set alloyed with ~0.5 at.% W. Conduct systematic ball-on-disk sliding tests under controlled dry conditions at multiple temperatures (e.g., RT, 400 °C, 800 °C). Use identical loads, sliding speeds, and counterface materials. Analyze the friction coefficient in real time and measure wear volumes post-test using profilometry and microscopy.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) vs. temperature and sliding cycles
Wear rate (mm³/N·m) quantified from wear track profiles
Microstructural and chemical analysis of worn surfaces (using SEM, EDS, and possibly TEM) to identify and characterize the presence and continuity of any tribo-oxide glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-alloyed samples do not consistently exhibit a significantly lower and more stable friction coefficient and reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range compared to the baseline samples—and if microstructural analysis fails to show the formation of a coherent, W-influenced oxide glaze layer—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

It was shown that Nb dissolves most WC particles and generates NbC, which enhances the solid solution strengthening effect of the CoCrFeNi HEA/WC cladding layer. Compared with the CoCrFeNi HEA coating, the hardness of the coating with Nb element is increased by 1.40 times, and the wear rate is reduced by 62.6%, which effectively reduces the peeling of the hard phase during wear. (5) The improvement in the corrosion resistance of the coating with Nb is not outstanding. The CoCrFeNi HEA/WC cladding coating with the addition of only WC particles has the largest curve, the smallest corrosion current, and the largest impedance, indicating that the CoCrFeNi HEA/WC cladding coating has the best corrosion resistance.

AbstractFriction and wear properties of hot working die steel at above 800 °C are of particular interest for high temperature applications. Here, novel AlCoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have been fabricated on the surface of hot working die steel by laser cladding. The effects of the as-prepared AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings on the microstructure and high temperature friction and wear behavior of hot working die steel are investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS). Having benefited from the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds after the addition of W elements, the high temperature wear resistance of the coatings is obviously improved, and friction coefficient shows a large fluctuation. The microstructural characteristics of the AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings after the high temperature wear resistance test shows a highly favorable impact on microstructure stability and wear resistance, due to its the strong lattice distortion effect of W element on BCC solid solutions and the second phase strengthening of the W-rich intermetallic compounds. cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 shows the influence of the W powder addition on the high temperature friction and wear properties of the AlCoCrFeNiWx coatings on H13 steel. The H13 steel exhibits a maximum friction coefficient and wear loss after 800 °C/60 min high temperature friction and wear treatment. Compared to the H13 steel, all HEA coatings exhibit smaller friction coefficient and wear loss. A minimum friction coefficient and wear loss (only 12% of H13 steel wear loss) occurs in the AlCoCrFeNiWx with the addition of 0.5 at.% W. Consequently, a great improvement in the high temperature friction and wear resistance is achieved by the addition of the W powder and is likely due to the lattice distortion becoming more remarkable; the unmelted W-rich particles also improve the wear resistance as the hard phase. The addition of 0.5 at.% W powder in AlCoCrFeNi HEA system can improve its high temperature friction and wear resistance. These results are also supported by wear scars height and width of samples. The distinct differences are observed with regard to three-dimensional morphologies, as shown in Figure 7.
